column1: In the paper-plane simulation, what is one story point?
column2: One paper plane that passes the Product Owner's acceptance criteria.

column1: In the simulation, what is velocity?
column2: The number of planes accepted in a single sprint.

column1: Who had sole acceptance authority in the simulation?
column2: The lecturer, playing the Product Owner.

column1: How long was the sprint execution timebox in the simulation?
column2: Five minutes.

column1: What was each team told to pick, and what was that role's job?
column2: A Scrum Master, to facilitate things and remove any obstacles.

column1: List the sprint 1 acceptance criteria.
column2: Flies straight; no spin during flight; travels up to 2 metres; passes the PO's aesthetics judgement.

column1: Which sprint 1 acceptance criterion was subjective?
column2: Aesthetics — a pass/fail judged entirely by the Product Owner.

column1: Why is a subjective acceptance criterion instructive?
column2: It cannot be encoded as a test in advance, so it can only be satisfied by understanding the customer.

column1: What two acceptance criteria were added in sprint 2?
column2: Hit a target on the wall, and carry the team's company logo.

column1: Did the sprint 1 criteria still apply in sprint 2?
column2: Yes — the change was additive, not a replacement.

column1: Give Team D's sprint 1 estimate and actual.
column2: Estimated 8, delivered 3.

column1: Give Team A's sprint 1 estimate and actual.
column2: Estimated 3, delivered 1.

column1: How many planes did Team D actually build in sprint 1, and how many passed?
column2: Nine built, three accepted.

column1: Which team had the highest velocity and still got the harshest verdict? Why?
column2: Team D — a large, repeated gap between what they estimated and what they delivered.

column1: Why does a persistent estimate-delivery gap matter more than low velocity?
column2: The Product Owner plans around your estimates; a team that reliably delivers three is more useful than one that promises eight and delivers three.

column1: What is the prescribed response to a repeated estimate gap?
column2: Discuss it with the team in the review and retrospective and figure out how to rectify it — not simply work harder next sprint.

column1: Which team beat its estimate in sprint 2?
column2: Team D — promised five, delivered six.

column1: What happened to Team C's sprint 2 output?
column2: Every plane was rejected; the whole team forgot the company logo.

column1: Why did last year's cohort produce far more planes under near-identical rules?
column2: The no-spin criterion was absent, and their smaller planes hit the target more often.

column1: What does the last-year comparison imply about velocity?
column2: Velocity is not comparable across different definitions of done.

column1: State the rule about sprint length.
column2: An important aspect of Scrum is that we never alter the sprint lengths — they must be exactly the same.

column1: What provoked the sprint-length rule in the simulation?
column2: Teams had started building planes during sprint 2's planning window.

column1: Why is the sprint boundary fixed while the events inside it flex?
column2: The boundary is what makes velocity comparable between sprints and lets the PO plan a release; internal timeboxes exist for focus, not measurement.

column1: Give two reasons not to extend a sprint that is overrunning.
column2: It impacts all later sprints and the overall project timeline, and it destroys velocity comparability.

column1: Name the three requirement changes introduced for sprint 2.
column2: One extra sheet of paper, a target to hit, and a company logo on each plane.

column1: What made the sprint 2 requirement changes legitimate rather than scope creep?
column2: They came with a stated business reason, were additive rather than a pivot, and brought extra resources.

column1: Why were sprint 1's planes confiscated before sprint 2?
column2: So no un-accepted work carries over; each sprint's velocity is that sprint's alone.

column1: Whose responsibility is understanding the requirements?
column2: Every individual team member's, equally — explicitly not just the Scrum Master's.

column1: Why is "all three of us forgot the logo" a structural failure rather than carelessness?
column2: If everyone assumes someone else is tracking the requirements, nobody is, and the gap stays invisible until the review.

column1: Which Scrum pillar failed when a whole team missed one acceptance criterion?
column2: Inspection — nobody checked anyone else's work against the criteria.

column1: What does the lecturer call a team member who does not understand what is expected?
column2: A fake or dummy member.

column1: What could every team have done to prepare for the target, and did any of them?
column2: Practised throwing at a mock target anywhere in the room — none did.

column1: State the general engineering failure the missed targets illustrate.
column2: Your tests passed in an environment that differs from the one acceptance actually happens in.

column1: How did a student reframe the untested-target failure?
column2: As running the product into the prod environment where it didn't work as expected.

column1: Why does a failure in front of the customer cost more than the same failure found privately?
column2: The client is bothered by it — the demo failure damages confidence even though the defect is identical.

column1: What did Team B's role structure look like in sprint 1?
column2: A Scrum Master, two developers, and one member assigned to QA.

column1: What did Team B change for sprint 2, and why?
column2: Everyone became a developer, because a dedicated QA was idle while construction was the bottleneck under time pressure.

column1: What did Team B's role change recover?
column2: The aesthetics criterion they had failed in sprint 1.

column1: Name the two legitimate triggers for switching roles mid-project.
column2: Something isn't working with a team member, or a team member is unavailable.

column1: Why does self-organisation depend on the retrospective?
column2: It responds to observed bottlenecks, and the retrospective is where they get observed.

column1: How many designs should a team commit to?
column2: One, or at most two.

column1: What is the argument for converging on one design?
column2: You gain real expertise in it, rather than being a jack of all designs.

column1: What process failure lets designs proliferate?
column2: Every developer is free to carry their own design, so an alternative continues even after the team agrees another is better.

column1: How do you reconcile "explore options" with "commit to one design"?
column2: Explore in sprint 1, converge by sprint 2 — the objection is to exploration that never reaches a decision point.

column1: What is the real-project analogue of the multiple-designs problem?
column2: Carrying two competing technology or architecture choices in parallel, so neither gains depth of expertise.

column1: What did late-joining members cost the teams?
column2: Sprint time spent catching them up, charged to the same timebox as the work.

column1: Is a member joining or returning mid-sprint an accident?
column2: No — the lecturer says it will also happen during your actual sprints.

column1: Name the two obligations when a member returns mid-project.
column2: Tell them where the development stands, and get them productive rather than merely informed.

column1: What ordering correction did the lecturer make between sprints?
column2: Run the sprint retrospective first, then sprint planning — "which is more natural".

column1: Why must the retrospective precede the next planning session?
column2: Its output is that session's input; reversed, the findings sit unused for a whole sprint.

column1: Give the full event order around a sprint boundary.
column2: Sprint, sprint review (product), sprint retrospective (team), sprint planning, next sprint.

column1: What replaced sprint 2's retrospective?
column2: A collective class retrospective — the whole-cohort debrief.

column1: State the Scrum leadership formula.
column2: Everyone is a leader and there is no leader; the Scrum Master is just a facilitator.

column1: What problem does a leaderless team create?
column2: With many views and nobody entitled to decide, decisions need genuine consensus — which requires everyone to have understood everyone else.

column1: Give the Scrum Master's job as a verb list.
column2: Keep looking, reviewing, tracking, monitoring how things are going.

column1: Which verbs are absent from the Scrum Master's job description?
column2: Decide, assign and approve.

column1: Why does one disengaged member damage a flat team disproportionately?
column2: It's not just lost capacity — it's a hole in the decision-making mechanism itself.

column1: What two process mistakes did the Product Owner admit to?
column2: Not forbidding building during sprint planning, and not supplying spare paper for testing.

column1: What did the missing test material cost the teams?
column2: They had to spend production material on experiments, so every test plane was a story point they couldn't deliver.

column1: Why does the PO's own mistake belong in the retrospective?
column2: Because velocity was partly a function of the PO's process design; a retrospective's target is the whole system, not just the team.

column1: What does "pilot error" refer to in the simulation?
column2: A defect in the demonstration rather than in the product — the plane was fine, the throw wasn't.

column1: Why is "pilot error" not a defence in front of a customer?
column2: The customer usually can't tell the difference between a bad product and a bad demo, and shouldn't have to.
